scenes.tts: Why can a moth population change colour even though no moth changes? Peppered moths rest on trunks and branches during the day. Some are pale and speckled. Others are nearly black. We will follow them through a woodland.
scenes.caption: Why can a moth population change colour even though no moth changes? Peppered moths rest on trunks and branches during the day. Some are pale and speckled. Others are nearly black. We will follow them through a woodland.
scenes.visual: Hook first. A daylit woodland fills most of the frame. Cream pale moths and blue-black dark moths settle on one large branch and trunk. A question mark grows from the mixed group. COLOUR MAP FOR BOTH FILMS: pale moths and less-emphasized plant forms = CREAM; dark moths and selected plant forms = BLUE-BLACK; survival and successful reproduction = GREEN; predation or removal = RED; deliberate human choice = TEAL. Label the whole film 'schematic'; do not show counts or percentages yet. Leaves drift and moth wings pulse slowly while narration continues.
scenes.narration: Why can a moth population change colour even though no moth changes? Peppered moths rest on trunks and branches during the day. Some are pale and speckled. Others are nearly black. We will follow them through a woodland.

scenes.visual: The woodland pulls back but remains behind a brief title, 'How a Population Changes Colour'. The title dissolves back into the same branch before the silent scene ends.

scenes.tts: The moths in this wood form a population: the same kind of living thing in one area. Each moth keeps its inherited wing colour for life. New variation first appears by chance. Natural selection works with variation already present.
scenes.caption: The moths in this wood form a population: the same kind of living thing in one area. Each moth keeps its inherited wing colour for life. New variation first appears by chance. Natural selection works with variation already present.
scenes.visual: A soft boundary draws around the woodland and gains the label 'population'. The mixed moths enlarge to fill the frame. Lock icons briefly appear beside each moth's colour, then fade. A small neutral sparkle enters beside the words 'variation appears by chance'; no moth changes colour.
scenes.narration: The moths in this wood form a population: the same kind of living thing in one area. Each moth keeps its inherited wing colour for life. New variation first appears by chance. Natural selection works with variation already present.

scenes.tts: Watch the blue-black and cream moths become parents. Their offspring usually share their colour because genes pass from parents to young. Real moths receive colour genes from both parents. This picture uses a simpler parent-to-offspring match.
scenes.caption: Watch the blue-black and cream moths become parents. Their offspring usually share their colour because genes pass from parents to young. Real moths receive colour genes from both parents. This picture uses a simpler parent-to-offspring match.
scenes.visual: The mixed moths move into a top row labelled 'parents'. Thin colour-matched paths lead toward a lower empty row labelled 'offspring'. Two parent icons briefly converge above each path to show the real two-parent refinement. The film then returns to simple cream-to-cream and blue-black-to-blue-black paths, labelled 'model simplification'.
scenes.narration: Watch the blue-black and cream moths become parents. Their offspring usually share their colour because genes pass from parents to young. Real moths receive colour genes from both parents. This picture uses a simpler parent-to-offspring match.

scenes.tts: Now the bark darkens with soot after pollution kills pale lichen. The environment includes everything around the moths, including bark, air, food and predators. A bird enters. It spots moths that stand out from the background more easily.
scenes.caption: Now the bark darkens with soot after pollution kills pale lichen. The environment includes everything around the moths, including bark, air, food and predators. A bird enters. It spots moths that stand out from the background more easily.
scenes.visual: Transform the same pale lichen-covered bark into dark sooty bark. Keep all moths fixed in colour and position. The pale moths gain high contrast; dark moths blend. A bird sweeps across the branch as four small labels orbit the scene: 'bark', 'air', 'food', 'predators', grouped under 'environment'.
scenes.narration: Now the bark darkens with soot after pollution kills pale lichen. The environment includes everything around the moths, including bark, air, food and predators. A bird enters. It spots moths that stand out from the background more easily.

scenes.tts: On this dark bark, which colour will birds find more often? Which colour will leave more young for the next generation?
scenes.caption: On this dark bark, which colour will birds find more often? Which colour will leave more young for the next generation?
scenes.visual: The bird pauses above the same dark branch. A large question card overlays the lower third: 'Which colour leaves more young?' Cream and blue-black moth groups glow in turn. Nothing is removed yet.
scenes.narration: On this dark bark, which colour will birds find more often? Which colour will leave more young for the next generation?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Hold the question and the two colour groups. A thin ring timer advances for the full pause while leaves continue a slow drift.

scenes.tts: The pale moths stand out, so the bird finds more of them. Dark moths are missed more often. More dark moths survive to reproduce. To reproduce means to have young. The survivors do not become better camouflaged. They already had their colour.
scenes.caption: The pale moths stand out, so the bird finds more of them. Dark moths are missed more often. More dark moths survive to reproduce. To reproduce means to have young. The survivors do not become better camouflaged. They already had their colour.
scenes.visual: The bird removes several CREAM moths along RED curved paths. Remaining moths gain small GREEN outlines. The BLUE-BLACK survivors move forward without changing colour. Show a crossed-out recolouring arrow beside one survivor, then clear it.
scenes.narration: The pale moths stand out, so the bird finds more of them. Dark moths are missed more often. More dark moths survive to reproduce. To reproduce means to have young. The survivors do not become better camouflaged. They already had their colour.

scenes.tts: Move the survivors into a parent row. Their offspring fill the woodland again. A generation is the step from parents to offspring. The new row contains a larger share of dark moths, although every individual kept its original colour.
scenes.caption: Move the survivors into a parent row. Their offspring fill the woodland again. A generation is the step from parents to offspring. The new row contains a larger share of dark moths, although every individual kept its original colour.
scenes.visual: GREEN-outlined survivors slide into the parent row. Colour-matched paths fill the offspring row below. A bracket between rows is labelled 'generation'. The lower row has visibly more BLUE-BLACK moths than the earlier row, but each icon retains one colour throughout.
scenes.narration: Move the survivors into a parent row. Their offspring fill the woodland again. A generation is the step from parents to offspring. The new row contains a larger share of dark moths, although every individual kept its original colour.

scenes.tts: How common a trait is in a population is called trait frequency, often written as a percent. Advance the woodland through more generations. On this sooty bark, the dark share usually grows as the same difference repeats.
scenes.caption: How common a trait is in a population is called trait frequency, often written as a percent. Advance the woodland through more generations. On this sooty bark, the dark share usually grows as the same difference repeats.
scenes.visual: The offspring row becomes a wide population strip. A brace labelled 'trait frequency' tracks the BLUE-BLACK share. Several new rows slide upward like a time belt; the blue-black section usually widens. Mark the animation 'schematic' and show no computed values.
scenes.narration: How common a trait is in a population is called trait frequency, often written as a percent. Advance the woodland through more generations. On this sooty bark, the dark share usually grows as the same difference repeats.

scenes.tts: Now clean the air and let pale lichen grow back. The bark becomes lighter. Dark moths now stand out more, so birds remove a larger share. The direction can reverse. Dark moths became rarer again in Britain and parts of the United States.
scenes.caption: Now clean the air and let pale lichen grow back. The bark becomes lighter. Dark moths now stand out more, so birds remove a larger share. The direction can reverse. Dark moths became rarer again in Britain and parts of the United States.
scenes.visual: Transform the same branch back to pale lichen bark. Increase contrast around BLUE-BLACK moths. The bird now follows RED paths toward more dark moths. The population strip reverses direction and its blue-black share narrows. A small map outline highlights Britain and parts of the United States without adding dates or values.
scenes.narration: Now clean the air and let pale lichen grow back. The bark becomes lighter. Dark moths now stand out more, so birds remove a larger share. The direction can reverse. Dark moths became rarer again in Britain and parts of the United States.

scenes.tts: A trait shaped by natural selection that helps survival and reproduction is an adaptation. Dark colour helped on sooty bark, not pale bark. Whether a trait helps depends on the environment. Moving individuals can pass genes into another population. That is gene flow, a different process.
scenes.caption: A trait shaped by natural selection that helps survival and reproduction is an adaptation. Dark colour helped on sooty bark, not pale bark. Whether a trait helps depends on the environment. Moving individuals can pass genes into another population. That is gene flow, a different process.
scenes.visual: Split the carried woodland into sooty and pale bark halves. The same BLUE-BLACK moth gains a GREEN outline only on the sooty side. Label the relationship 'adaptation depends on environment'. Then a separate moth crosses the woodland boundary into a neighbouring woodland and joins its parent row, along a neutral arrow labelled 'gene flow: genes move between populations', kept visually apart from the bird filter.
scenes.narration: A trait shaped by natural selection that helps survival and reproduction is an adaptation. Dark colour helped on sooty bark, not pale bark. Whether a trait helps depends on the environment. Moving individuals can pass genes into another population. That is gene flow, a different process.

scenes.tts: This is natural selection. Individuals whose inherited traits suit their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce. Inherited traits that help survival and reproduction become more common over generations. The rule describes a population, not a moth changing.
scenes.caption: This is natural selection. Individuals whose inherited traits suit their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce. Inherited traits that help survival and reproduction become more common over generations. The rule describes a population, not a moth changing.
scenes.visual: Return to the complete carried picture: mixed parent row, bird filter on bark, GREEN survivors, and shifted offspring row. A moving bracket travels from 'inherited variation' through 'different reproduction' to 'trait frequency changes'. Hold on the population while individual moth colours remain locked.
scenes.narration: This is natural selection. Individuals whose inherited traits suit their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce. Inherited traits that help survival and reproduction become more common over generations. The rule describes a population, not a moth changing.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex and one line only: 'Inherited traits that help survival and reproduction become more common over generations.'
